title: Study Shows Impact of Binge Drinking on Young Brains
paragraphs: Binge drinking isn't good for anyone, but it's particularly harmful to adolescents, and could have a serious impact on their long-term brain health.
A study in Molecular Psychiatry took a closer look at how binge drinking could affect the adolescent brain, finding that it may cause lasting changes that persist into adulthood.

The researchers exposed adolescent rats to pure ethanol — the type of alcohol we drink — in a similar way to how humans binge drink. That meant giving them high levels of ethanol in a short amount of time, with either one or two days between sessions.
The researchers found that binge-like exposure to alcohol had a significant effect on how the rats' brains worked.
They found evidence of disrupted communications between synapses in the hippocampus — a region of the brain important for learning and memory — and brain cells called astrocytes.

Astrocytes are only beginning to be understood by scientists, but we know they play an important role in the healthy formation of synapses, which are tiny connections in the brain that allow information to flow from one neuron to another.

The researchers found that these disruptions weren't just temporary, but lasted into adulthood, which could explain why binge drinking at a young age is linked with poorer long-term cognitive and mental health outcomes in humans.

"Understanding why binge drinking specifically during adolescence worsens mental health outcomes and reduces overall quality of life is the goal of this research," explained study co-author Mary-Louise Risher from Marshall University in West Virginia.

She added that the research could also help increase public awareness of the long-term dangers of teenage binge drinking, and inform the development of new approaches to treating and managing the damage it can do.
This is because the researchers also found that targeted treatments were able to improve communication between the rats' brain cells.
While this needs further research, similar treatments focused on improving astrocyte function in the human brain could address the ill effects of alcohol abuse among young people.
